To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of low tidal volume (6 ml/kg) is the only ventilator setting that has been demonstrated to improve mortality, while the use of higher positive end-expiracy pressure and lower driving pressures is still a matter of discussion.

the use of high tidal volume ventilation is associated with increased lung injury and mortality, and that the use of low tidal volume ventilation is the most effective strategy to minimize ventilator induced lung injury.
1) protective ventilation is mandatory in acute respiratory distress syndrome; and 2) super-protective ventilation may be considered in selected cases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of new approaches to minimize the ventilator-induced lung and extra-pulmonary injury in patients with acute lung injury/acute respiratory distress syndrome.
the search of new strategies to reduce the ventilatory support and to minimize the lung damage caused by mechanical ventilation.
the search of new ventilatory strategies that minimize lung damage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ‘best’ mechanical ventilation is the one that is able to minimize ventilator induced lung injury.
‘protective’ mechanical ventilation is a must, but it may not be enough to protect the lungs and the patient from the consequences of ventilator-induced biotrauma.
‘protective ventilation is mandatory and super-protective ventilation should be considered in patients with acute lung injury and acute respiratory distress syndrome’.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are now moving from the era of ‘best’ mechanical ventilation to ‘super-protect’ mechanical ventilation.
the best ventilator settings are those which allow to minimize lung damage, to improve oxygenation and lung mechanics and to reduce systemic inflammation.
‘protective ventilation’ is not a static goal, but a dynamic process that is constantly evolving.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ‘protective’ approach to mechanical ventilation is still the best approach to prevent ventilator-induced lung and organ injury.
the ‘protective’ ventilatory strategy is not a single strategy and the choice of the best approach should be tailored on the patient’s characteristics and on the clinical context.

‘super-protecting’ ventilation can be effective in reducing ventilator-induced lung and systemic injury and that it may be the next step to further reduce mortality in patients with acute lung injury and acute respiratory distress syndrome.
